body.value: This page explains the process of buying and maintaining a home in clear steps.
Check what you can afford to buy

Before you begin to look at properties, you need to find out how much you can afford to pay for your mortgage each month. You will also need to consider the monthly expenses that can come with owning a home, such as gas, electricity and internet bills. A budget planner can be a helpful tool to do this.

If you are applying for a mortgage, the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) has a mortgage calculator that shows what your monthly repayments will be with each provider depending on the amount you borrow, how long the mortgage will last and the interest rate. You also need to consider how much of a mortgage the lender might offer you.

Find out more about getting a mortgage.
Find out what supports are available for buying a home

If you’re looking to buy, a number of supports are available.

Help to Buy

If you are a first time buyer, the Help to Buy scheme can help you with a deposit for a new or self-build home. You receive a refund on income and DIRT tax paid in Ireland in the last four years.

First Home Scheme

For first time buyers, self-builders or those making a fresh start, this shared equity scheme provides finance to help you bridge the gap between a deposit and mortgage, and the price of a new home. This scheme takes a percentage ownership of your home, which you can buy back later.

Local Authority Home Loan

If you are a first time buyer or making a fresh start but have been unable to obtain finance from traditional mortgage providers, a Local Authority Home Loan can assist you to buy or build a home. You can borrow up to 90% of the property’s value.

Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant

Purchasers of vacant or derelict properties can receive up to €70,000 to turn a vacant house or building into a permanent home or a rental property with this grant.

Local Authority Affordable Purchase Scheme

For first time buyers or fresh starters, local authorities are making new homes available for purchase at reduced prices through a shared equity model.

Before you begin your property search, prepare the documents you may be asked for during the process. This can include photo ID, proof of income or employment, and your PPS Number.

As a buyer, you will be asked by mortgage providers for bank statements and information about your employment, such as a Salary Certificate and Employment Detail Summary. You will also need a solicitor.
Search for a property that meets your requirements

You can find homes that are available to purchase by searching property websites and contacting estate agents and auctioneers.

You can search the Residential Property Price Register to find out what price was paid for a property in the past. Learn more about things to keep in mind when house-hunting.
Prepare for moving from 'sale agreed' to 'sold'

When you have had an offer accepted, there are a few more steps you need to take before you own the property.

This can include paying a booking deposit to the estate agent, organising a building condition survey of the property and reviewing the letter of offer from your lender.

When you receive the contract of sale for the property, your solicitor will check that the contracts are in order, investigate the title documents and raise any necessary enquiries with the seller's solicitor. By signing the contracts, you are legally agreeing to buy the property and the seller is legally agreeing to sell it. If you withdraw from the sale after this contract has been signed, you may lose your deposit.

Your solicitor will also secure your property deed which shows the new ownership details, and organise payment of Stamp Duty to Revenue.

There are a number of utilities and bills that you will be responsible for as a homeowner. These can include:

  • gas
  • electricity
  • water
  • household waste disposal
  • telecoms
  • internet

In some cases, you may be able to organise these connections before you move in.

Most homeowners will also have to pay Local Property Tax (LPT), which is an annual tax charged on the market value of certain residential properties.
Supports available for running your home

Fuel Allowance

Depending on your situation, you may qualify for Fuel Allowance, which is a payment to help with the cost of heating your home during the winter months.

Household Benefits Package

The Household Benefits Package helps towards the costs of electricity or gas bills for those who qualify. It also includes a free TV licence.

SEAI grants

The Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) offers grants to homeowners and landlords to upgrade their homes' energy efficiency. This results in reduced energy use, costs and greenhouse gas emissions.

For landlords: Residential Premises Rental Income Relief (RPRIR)

Individual landlords of rented residential properties may be eligible for the Residential Premises Rental Income Relief (RPRIR).

Additionally, the Repair and Leasing Scheme (RLS) is an option for owners or purchasers of vacant properties who cannot afford or access the funding needed to bring their properties up to rental standards.
